messages.body_plain:
Hi Wang,

Once you have your object of class network, you can use the 
set.vertex.attribute() function to add vertex attributes. You can also 
use the wrapper "%v%". Here is a simple example:

# Initialize an empty network:
net<-network.initialize(7)

# Define a vertex attribute defining the age of each node:
nodeage<-c(10,12,10,11,9,13,14)
set.vertex.attribute(net,"age",nodeage)

#Or identically, you can do:
net %v% "age" <-nodeage

# To list all existing vertex attributes:
list.vertex.attributes(net)

Hope this helps,
Victorin

                Data.mat<-as.matrix(read.table("data.csv",header=FALSE,sep=",")

Hi Philip,

> First, how do I attach covariates to the 10 by 10 matrix?

To attach covariates to an object of class network, you can use the 
set.vertex.attribute() function. For example:

nodeage<-c(10,12,10,11,9,13,14,23,21,21) # age of each node:
set.vertex.attribute(Data.net,"age",nodeage)

Identically, you could use:

Data.net %v% "age"<-nodeage

> The second question is how do I label the vertices in the matrix?

When you list the existing attributes in you network object, you see 
that a "vertex.name" atttribute already exist:

list.vertex.attributes(Data.net) #list existing vertex attributes
get.vertex.attribute(Data.net,"vertex.names")

To replace the default values:

names<-c("A","B","C","D","E","F","G","H","I","J")
set.vertex.attribute(Data.net,"vertex.names",names)

Identically:

Data.net %v% "vertex.names"<-names

> Can someone direct me to, ?Getting Data Loaded into Statnet For Dummies??

Since the network objects used by Statnet are of class "network" (this 
class is defined in the network package), I recommend you to read: 
Butts, C. T. (2008). network: a Package for Managing Relational Data in 
R. Journal of Statistical.

See also the help pages:
help(attribute.methods)

Hope this will help,

Hello Everyone,
I was running a simple nodemix model and getting some interesting results.  I have a directed network with 358 vertices and 353 edges.  I have several binary node classifications coded as vertex attributes (where around 45-50 vertices are classified with a 1 and the rest with a 0). I am several different node mixing models, such as: ergm(allnet~nodemix("a")), ergm(allnet~nodemix("b")), ergm(allnet~nodemix("a")+nodecov("z")), etc...

My classification of interest ("a") is yielding the same estimate (and standard error) for both mixed pairings.  This is regardless of whether I include any nodecov terms.  I have printed an example below:

mix.a.0.0 -6.50457    0.08311        NA  <1e-04 ***
mix.a.1.0 -5.26241    0.11655        NA  <1e-04 ***
mix.a.0.1 -5.26241    0.11655        NA  <1e-04 ***
mix.a.1.1 -3.65862    0.14045        NA  <1e-04 ***


When I run the other classification ("b"). I don't get this same result.  Maybe this is just the luck of the draw, but a part of me (and I know reviewers) has a hard time believing that the log-odds of a directed tie from 1 to 0 is the exact same as 0 to 1.  Is there anything that might explain this?  

I have also tabulated the number of connection types (and ensured there wasn't a coding error where the 1.0 ties are the same as the 0.1 ties):
0.0 147
1.0  77
0.1  75
1.1 118


Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated!
Jared

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola.   Are you familiar with the manuscript that introduces this  
stepping idea?  An earlier version is available at http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/tr1003.pdf 
  and it will be coming out sometime soon in J Comp Graph Stat.

Even if you are familiar with it, the error might still need a bit of  
explanation.  Ideally, the stepping algorithm uses a series of "steps"  
to gradually close in on the MLE.  When it gets close enough so that  
it appears plain MCMCMLE can be used to get a final estimate, the  
algorithm draws one more large sample for this final estimate.  If,  
for some reason, the observed vector of statistics is not contained  
inside the convex hull of sampled statistics, then the approximate MLE  
will not exist (and somehow the stepping algorithm didn't quite do its  
job even though it believed that it had done so).  The default  
behavior of the code at this point is to throw the error you're seeing.

I hope this explains it.

Best,
Dave
